Stratified sampling

Source: R/design-stratified.R
design_stratified.Rd

Draws a sample from each stratum. Allocation uses the largest-remainder method, so the returned row count matches n exactly rather than drifting with per-stratum rounding.

Usage

design_stratified(
  strata,
  n,
  allocation = c("proportional", "equal", "neyman"),
  allocation_by = NULL,
  min_per_stratum = 0L,
  replace = FALSE,
  na_rm = FALSE,
  cost = NULL,
  within = NULL
)

Arguments

strata

One or more column names defining the strata. Several columns are cross-classified.

n

Total rows to draw across all strata, under any allocation, or a plan from plan_size(). With counts in allocation it can be left out and is their sum; when given, it must equal that sum.

allocation

How n is split across strata: a rule, or the count for each stratum. Of the rules, "proportional" gives each stratum a share of n in proportion to its size; "equal" splits n evenly; "neyman" gives shares proportional to size * sd, with the standard deviation of each stratum from allocation_by (Neyman 1934). Neyman minimises the variance of a total for a fixed n by putting more rows where the values vary most, and is the right choice when you have a frame variable correlated with what you are measuring, or estimates of each stratum's standard deviation from a pilot or an earlier survey. Under any rule, a stratum that would be allocated more rows than it holds is taken whole, one that would get fewer than min_per_stratum gets that many, and the rest of n is re-split over the others by the same rule (Cochran 1977, section 5.9).

Counts are a named vector, such as c(north = 10, south = 5, east = 5), when strata is one column, its names matched to that column's values as text; or a data frame holding the strata columns and a column n, matched on the values themselves. Every stratum of the frame needs a count, 0 included, and a count for a stratum the frame does not have is refused, so a misspelt name cannot quietly leave a stratum out. Without replacement no count may exceed the rows in its stratum. The design then draws exactly those counts, and the inclusion probabilities, variances and as_svydesign() follow them.

allocation_by

The standard deviation of each stratum, for allocation = "neyman". Ignored otherwise. Either a column of the frame, whose standard deviation within each stratum is used, and which needs a finite value on every row allocated over; or the standard deviations themselves, so the frame needs no such column. Those are a named vector, such as c(north = 40, south = 15), when strata is one column, its names matched to that column's values as text; or a data frame holding the strata columns and a column sd, matched on the values themselves. Every stratum of the frame needs one, and each must be finite and 0 or more. A value for a stratum the frame does not have is ignored, so the same values serve a part of the frame, such as the rest of design_certainty() when every row of a stratum is above the threshold. A stratum with a standard deviation of 0 gets no share.

min_per_stratum

Minimum rows from each stratum, under an allocation rule. With the default of 0, a stratum smaller than about N / n can be allocated no rows at all; its rows then have inclusion probability 0 and a total estimated from the sample silently leaves them out, so draw() warns when that happens. 1 makes every stratum reachable, which is what an unbiased Horvitz-Thompson total needs, and 2 also lets every stratum contribute to the variance estimate. Over-sampling a small stratum this way does not bias an estimate made with the design weights, which correct for it; it only moves precision around. Without replacement a stratum smaller than the floor is taken whole, so n must cover min_per_stratum rows from each stratum, or all of a smaller one. With counts in allocation, give each stratum its count there instead.

replace

Sample with replacement within each stratum?

na_rm

Drop rows whose stratum key is NA instead of raising an error.

cost

The cost of sampling one row in each stratum, for allocation = "neyman" only. In the same forms as standard deviations given in allocation_by, with the column of a data frame named cost, so one data frame of the strata columns, sd and cost can serve both. Each must be finite and above 0. The shares become proportional to size * sd / sqrt(cost), which gives the smallest variance among the splits of the same total cost, sum(cost * n_h) over strata (Cochran 1977, section 5.5). Before any stratum is held at its floor or its size, the n that spends a budget C, net of any fixed cost, is C * sum(N_h * S_h / sqrt(c_h)) / sum(N_h * S_h * sqrt(c_h)), rounded down. When no stratum has any spread, the shares are proportional to size / sqrt(cost), as for equal spreads, and without cost to size.

within

How rows are drawn inside each stratum: NULL, the default, for a simple random sample, or design_systematic() without interval or n, to walk each stratum in the order of its order_by column, or in frame order without one. Each stratum gets the rows the allocation gives it, at an even step from a random start of its own; see "Systematic sampling within strata". Needs replace = FALSE.

Value

A design object, for use with draw(). allocation_table() shows the rows it takes from each stratum of a frame before anything is drawn.

Rounding, ties and the order of strata

Each stratum first gets the whole part of its share of n. The rows left over go one at a time to the strata with the largest fractional parts. When two strata tie, the one with more rows not yet allocated goes first, and after that the one that comes first in key order. min_per_stratum and the size of each stratum bound the shares before they are rounded, so the rounding never takes a stratum below its floor or past its size.

Key order is the order of the levels for a factor column and the sorted values for any other column, with text sorted byte by byte as in the C locale ("B" before "a"). With several strata columns the first varies slowest. Strata are also drawn from in this order, so a seed selects the same rows in every locale. Renaming a stratum, or reordering a factor's levels, can move a tied row from one stratum to another; the inclusion probabilities always follow the allocation used.

An empty string is a stratum like any other, shown as (blank) in messages.

Systematic sampling within strata

With within = design_systematic(order_by = "x"), the strata are allocated as without it, each stratum is sorted on x, and the n_h rows allocated to a stratum of N_h are taken as design_systematic(n = n_h) takes them from a frame of N_h rows: a start drawn from (0, 1) and a step of N_h / n_h rows, which need not be whole. Strata draw their starts in key order. Every row has probability n_h / N_h, as under simple random sampling within strata, so the allocation, allocation_table() and the weights are the same; what changes is which rows can be drawn together. Two rows of one stratum have the joint probability of the systematic design there, which is 0 for rows at most N_h / n_h - 1 rows apart, and two rows of different strata the product of their probabilities. Rows whose x is missing are refused, or with the na_rm = TRUE of the systematic design left out of their stratum before it is allocated.

Each stratum has one random start, so when any stratum is walked at a step of 2 rows or more no design-unbiased variance exists, as for design_systematic() on its own. ht_total() and ht_mean() add up the strata's successive-difference approximations, (1 - n_h / N_h) * n_h / (2 * (n_h - 1)) * sum(diff(y / pi)^2) over each stratum's sampled rows in the order it was walked (Wolter 2007), with the degrees of freedom of a stratified sample, the sampled rows less the strata. A stratum with one sampled row from several is refused, as without within. So is the jackknife: a stratum's rows all come from one start, and deleting them one at a time does not mirror the design. as_svydesign() hands survey the strata, whose simple-random variance differs.

Only design_systematic() is taken as within, with one start and no interval or n: the allocation sets the size of each stratum. To walk a stratum by several columns, give order_by a column of ranks, as in the examples of design_systematic().

References

Neyman, J. (1934). On the two different aspects of the representative method: the method of stratified sampling and the method of purposive selection. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, 97, 558–625. doi:10.2307/2342192

Cochran, W. G. (1977). Sampling Techniques, 3rd ed. Wiley.

Wolter, K. M. (2007). Introduction to Variance Estimation, 2nd ed. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-0-387-35099-8

See also

draw(), allocation_table()

Other designs: design_bootstrap(), design_certainty(), design_cluster(), design_multistage(), design_reservoir(), design_simple(), design_spatial(), design_spread(), design_systematic(), design_temporal(), design_weighted()

Examples

df <- data.frame(id = 1:100, site = rep(letters[1:4], each = 25))
table(draw(df, design_stratified("site", n = 20), seed = 1)$site)
#> 
#> a b c d 
#> 5 5 5 5 

# Rare strata are covered only if you ask -- without the floor, the one
# "rare" row gets no allocation, and draw() warns that it is unreachable
skewed <- data.frame(id = 1:1000, g = c(rep("common", 999), "rare"))
draw(skewed, design_stratified("g", n = 10, min_per_stratum = 1), seed = 1)$g
#>  [1] "common" "common" "common" "common" "common" "common" "common" "common"
#>  [9] "common" "rare"  

# A count for each stratum, drawn as given; `n` is their sum
fixed <- design_stratified("site", allocation = c(a = 8, b = 4, c = 4, d = 4))
table(draw(df, fixed, seed = 1)$site)
#> 
#> a b c d 
#> 8 4 4 4 

# Neyman from standard deviations known from an earlier survey, with the
# cost of reaching a row in each stratum
pilot <- design_stratified("site", n = 20, allocation = "neyman",
                           allocation_by = c(a = 4, b = 1, c = 2, d = 8),
                           cost = c(a = 1, b = 1, c = 4, d = 4))
allocation_table(df, pilot)
#>   site  N n prob sd cost status
#> 1    a 25 8 0.32  4    1   rule
#> 2    b 25 2 0.08  1    1   rule
#> 3    c 25 2 0.08  2    4   rule
#> 4    d 25 8 0.32  8    4   rule

# Each stratum walked in order of `size`, from a start of its own
df$size <- (df$id * 37) %% 101
walked <- design_stratified("site", n = 20,
                            within = design_systematic(order_by = "size"))
draw(df, walked, seed = 1)
#>    id site size
#> 1   5    a   84
#> 2  10    a   67
#> 3  17    a   23
#> 4  22    a    6
#> 5  23    a   43
#> 6  27    b   90
#> 7  33    b    9
#> 8  39    b   29
#> 9  40    b   66
#> 10 45    b   49
#> 11 51    c   69
#> 12 57    c   89
#> 13 63    c    8
#> 14 69    c   28
#> 15 75    c   48
#> 16 77    d   21
#> 17 83    d   41
#> 18 89    d   61
#> 19 90    d   98
#> 20 95    d   81
